tootik is federated using ActivityPub: users can join an existing instance or set up their own, then interact with users on the same instance and users of compatible servers like Mastodon, Lemmy, Sharkey, Friendica, Akkoma, GoToSocial, Mitra and PieFed.
Unlike other social networks, tootik doesn't have a browser-based interface or an app: instead, its minimalistic, text-based interface is served over Gemini:
* Its UI is Gemini-based: there's a wide variety of clients to choose from and some work great on old devices.
* It's a single static executable, making it easy to set up your own instance and update it later.
* All instance data is stored in a single file, a sqlite database that is easy to backup and restore.
* It's written from scratch (not forked from some other project) in two languages (Go and SQL), making the codebase suitable for educational purposes and easy to hack on.
* Good compatibility with various fediverse servers
* FEP-044f quote posts, without support for approval
* With support for manual approval of follow requests
* With support for Mastodon's follower synchronization mechanism, aka FEP-8fcf
* Accounts on different servers use one Ed25519 or ML-DSA-44 keypair
* User activity is replicated across all servers
* Mention community in a public post to start thread
* Community sends posts and replies to all members
* Upload of posts and user avatars, over Titan
You can join an existing instance or set up your own.

3. `persons`, which contains Actor objects that represent users
Federation happens through two tables, `inbox` and `outbox`. Both contain Activity objects that represent actions performed by the users in `persons`.
gemini.Listener is a Gemini server that handles requests using Handler. It adds rows to `persons` during new user registration and changes rows when users change properties like their display name.

gemini.Listener provides Handler with a writer that builds a Gemini response and asynchronously sends it to the client in chunks, while Handler continues to handle the request and append more lines to the page.
User actions like post creation or deletion are recorded as Activity objects written to `outbox`.
fed.Queue polls `outbox` and delivers these activities to followers on other servers. It uses the `deliveries` table to track delivery progress and retry failed deliveries.

Resolver is responsible for fetching Actors that represent users of other servers, using an ID or a `user@domain` pair and WebFinger. The fetched objects are cached in `persons`, and contain properties like the user's inbox URL and public key.

fed.Queue uses Resolver to make a list of unique inbox URLs each activity should be delivered to. If this is a wide delivery (a public post or a post to followers) and multiple recipients reside on the same server, fed.Queue delivers the activity to this server only once.
Requests from other servers are handled by fed.Listener, a HTTP server.

It extracts the signature and key ID from a request using httpsig.Extract, uses Resolver to fetch the public key if needed, validates the request using Verify and inserts the received Activity object into `inbox`.
Once inserted into `inbox`, inbox.Queue processes the received activities:
Sometimes, a received or newly created local Activity is forwarded to the followers of a local user:
* When a remote user replies in a thread started by a local user, the received Activity is inserted into `outbox` and forwarded to all followers of the local user.
* When a user creates a new post, edits a post or deletes a post in a local community, the Activity is inserted into `outbox` and forwarded to all community members.
To display details like the user's name and speed up the verification of future incoming replies, inbox.Queue uses Resolver to fetch the Actor objects of mentioned users (if needed).

To speed up each user's feed, inbox.FeedUpdater periodically appends rows to the `feed` table. This table holds all information that appears in the user's feed: posts written or shared by followed users, author information and more, eliminating the need for `join` queries, slow filtering by post visibility, deduplication and sorting by time when a user views their feed. This table is indexed by user and time, allowing fast querying of a single feed page for a particular user.

The cluster package contains complex tests that simulate interaction between users on multiple servers. These tests are easy to write, they're fast and they run in parallel without affecting each other.
The tests use three main constructs: Client, Server and Cluster.
During tests, all http.Requests sent by tootik (like those sent by fed.Resolver) are sent through Client.
Server handles all kinds of incoming requests:
* Wraps net.Pipe with TLS and gemini.Listener to allow tests to simulate interaction with the Gemini interface, including user authentication through client certificates
* It uses the same http.Handler as fed.Listener to handle an incoming http.Request but without needing an actual HTTP server
Client holds a mapping between domain names and Servers: it allows these servers to talk to each other by passing the http.Request sent by one server to the http.Handler of another.
Cluster is a high-level wrapper for easy creation of multiple Servers capable of federating with each other, given a list of domain names.

Routes, scopes, events, requests, jobs and configuration for each module are in `docs/modules.md`.

|Configuration-driven modules|`modules.json` lists the enabled modules (`"*"` for all). Modules are found by assembly scan and start in an explicit priority order. Outbox and BackgroundJobs are core modules that always load.|
|Compiler-enforced boundaries|No module project references another. Architecture tests and a commit guard fail the build the moment one does.|
|DDD on writes, vertical slices on reads|Writes go endpoint, aggregate method, domain event, save. Reads project straight into DTOs with `AsNoTracking`.|

|REPR minimal APIs|One folder per feature: `Endpoint.cs`, `Request.cs` with its validator inline, `Response.cs`. URL-segment API versioning (`/v1/...`); IAM and Notifications routes are version neutral.|

|Railway-oriented code|A `Result<T>` monad with `BindAsync`, `TapAsync`, `MapAsync` and `CombineAsync`. Errors carry a key, a parameter, a value and an HTTP status, and become localized `ProblemDetails`.|
|Strongly typed ids|Ids are value types with EF converters, route binding and a Swagger schema filter. A test forbids reaching into `.Value` inside a query.|
|Versioned, frozen domain events|A shipped `V1` event never changes. New shapes ship as `V2`. A contract test enforces which payload types an event may carry.|
|Database per module|Each module owns a `DbContext` and a PostgreSQL schema. Point its connection string at another server to split the data.|

|Transactional outbox|Events are written in the same transaction as the state change. The processor claims batches with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, publishes in parallel, retries with backoff, cleans up after itself and exports lag metrics.|

|Transactional inbox|Consumers inherit `IntegrationEventHandlerBase<T>`: a FusionCache pre-filter plus a `ProcessedMessages` row committed with the handler's own save. A scheduled job prunes old rows.|
|Event coalescing|Events implementing `ICoalescableIntegrationEvent` collapse into one outbox row per type and key per save, so a bulk change does not become a message storm.|

|Inter-module requests|`IInterModuleRequestClient<TRequest, TResponse>` runs over MassTransit request/response, with per-request timeouts and a dedicated receive endpoint per handler. A timeout reaches the HTTP client as `503` with `Retry-After`, a handler fault as `502`.|
|No ordering assumptions|Delivery order is never guaranteed. Ready-made projection building blocks (`ProjectionEntity`, `UpsertIfNewerAsync`) drop stale events, and a reconciliation job heals drift.|
|Trace context across hops|The trace context is stored with each outbox row and sent with the message, so a consumer in another process can continue the same trace.|

|Keycloak, realm as code|Users, roles, clients, flows, authorization services and seed users live in `keycloak/realm-modular-monolith.json`. Compose, tests and production start import the same file. Clients only talk to this API.|

|Two login schemes|Phone + SMS OTP for end users, email + password with email verification for staff. `identityScheme.json` picks which self-service registration and login routes exist (`PhoneNumber` or `Email`).|

|Fine-grained permissions|Endpoints declare `.RequireScope(KeycloakScopes.X.Y)`. The API asks Keycloak for a `resource#scope` decision with the caller's token and caches it per token. An administration read asks `-view-all`, its owner twin `-view-own`; one right is held by a realm role policy (`store-owner`). A test keeps code and realm in sync.|
|Sessions and devices|Every login binds a device and client. Users can list their sessions, revoke one or revoke all. Access tokens live 5 minutes and refresh tokens rotate.|
|Token reuse defence|Replaying a rotated refresh token revokes the whole user session and sends the user a security alert push.|
|Machine callers|A client-credentials sample (`ci-integration`) shows service-to-service access through a service account policy.|
|Optional captcha|reCAPTCHA with a score threshold behind the `IAM.Captcha` feature flag. A `Dummy` provider passes everything in development.|
|EF Core 10 on PostgreSQL|One `DbContext` per module, queries tagged with `TagWith`, unique-violation mapping through `EntityFrameworkCore.Exceptions`.|
|Multilingual full-text search|Per-row authored language, generated `tsvector` columns with GIN indexes, accent folding, relevance ranking. See `docs/full-text-search.md`.|
|Trigram and pattern indexes|`HasTrigramIndex` and `HasPatternIndex` plus `LikePattern.Contains` and `LikePattern.StartsWith` for names, codes and barcodes a user types a fragment of.|

|Automatic audit trail|Every domain event an aggregate raises is stored in `AuditLog` (type, version, payload, actor) in the same transaction. A retention job prunes it (90 days by default, per-schema overrides) and history endpoints page it with a keyset cursor.|
|Offset and keyset pagination|`PageNumber`/`PageSize` or an opaque `After` cursor with a tiebreaker. `IncludeTotal=false` skips the `COUNT(*)`.|
|S3-compatible object storage|A public store for CDN-cached objects and a private store with presigned upload and download URLs. Circuit breaker, retries and multipart uploads are configurable.|
|Caching|FusionCache with a size-bounded in-memory L1. Switch on Redis for an L2 and a backplane, with fail-safe settings for slow or failing sources.|
|Seeding|Ordered `IDatabaseSeeder`s run after the host has fully started.|

|Queued jobs|Accept, queue, poll: `JobRow`, an atomic claim, 202 answers, bounded batches with a stored cursor, a stuck-job sweep and housekeeping. Worked examples: product import and export, stock bulk adjustment.|

|Spreadsheets and CSV|Uploaded `.xlsx` and `.xls` files are read in batches (ExcelDataReader) with a row ceiling, row-level rejections and a stored list of the first errors. A CSV writer guards against formula injection, and the file is served as a download.|

|Secret protection|`SecretProtector` encrypts credentials a module must read back (AES-GCM, key from `secretProtection.json`, key id in every value so the key can be rotated through `PreviousEncryptionKeys`), and `SecretGenerator` invents the secrets a caller presents back.|

|Rate limiting|Named fixed-window policies (global, SMS, email, OTP verify, registration, registration check, token create and refresh, own-store creation, store application, warehouse webhook). With Redis configured every replica shares one counter, without it an in-process limiter takes over. Each policy chooses to fail open or closed.|

|Keyed resilience pipelines|Outbound HTTP gets timeouts, retries and circuit breakers from `ResiliencyOptions`, with keyed overrides per dependency. The warehouse gateway builds one pipeline per store connection, without a retry for calls that change state, and its HTTP client refuses addresses that lead into the server's own network (no private, loopback or link-local target, no redirects, no proxy).|

|Webhook hardening|Constant-time HMAC-SHA256 verification (hex or base64, with or without `sha256=`), a secret per connection, a request body size limit, a per-connection rate limit, each delivery applied once through a delivery id table, and statuses applied in the order of the provider's own timestamp.|
|Reverse proxy support|Forwarded headers honoured only from configured trusted networks.|
|Request and response logging|Size-capped body logging with per-path redaction for tokens, OTP codes, registrations, store applications and warehouse connection credentials, and path exclusions.|
|Feature management|`Microsoft.FeatureManagement` with targeting and variants, plus a `.RequireFeature(...)` endpoint filter.|

|Health checks|Separate live, ready, startup and dependency probes. PostgreSQL, RabbitMQ and Redis (when configured) gate readiness. Keycloak is reported on the dependency probe only, and only in a process that runs the IAM module, so an outage never takes the whole API out of rotation.|
|SMS, email, push|NetGSM, Brevo and Firebase Cloud Messaging adapters. Each has a `Dummy` provider that logs instead of sending, which startup validation rejects in Production.|
|OTP with quotas|Configurable code length, expiry, resend interval and per-recipient and daily send caps. Templates are localized.|
|SignalR hub|`/hubs/notifications` for authenticated users, with an optional Redis backplane that production configuration requires by default.|

|**Query plans**|Explore supported EXPLAIN output as a tree or graph, inspect step details and compare plans. PostgreSQL plans include timing, row-estimate comparisons and insights.|
|**Schema diagrams**|Explore tables and foreign keys with crow's-foot relationships, keys-only views and saved card positions.|
